title: Grids & Grid-and-Compute
description: TSO/DSO roles, frequency & inertia, congestion/redispatch, zonal vs nodal pricing, and siting flexible data-centre load on the grid.

cards.front: What's the split between a **TSO** and a **DSO**?
cards.back: **TSO** (e.g. TenneT) runs the **high-voltage backbone** — real-time balancing, frequency (50 Hz), security, reserves. **DSO** runs the **lower-voltage local** networks delivering power the last mile to end users.

cards.front: Why transmit power at **high voltage**, and where does **HVDC** win?
cards.back: High voltage cuts current and therefore **resistive losses** over long distances. **HVDC** is more efficient over very long distances and is essential for **sub-sea interconnectors** and linking asynchronous grids.

cards.front: What does it mean that European grid **frequency** must stay near 50 Hz?
cards.back: Frequency **rises** when generation exceeds demand and **falls** when demand exceeds generation. Holding it at 50 Hz is continuous real-time balancing, done with reserves (FCR/aFRR/mFRR) and cushioned by inertia.

cards.front: What is **congestion**, and how does a TSO fix it with **redispatch**?
cards.back: Congestion = the cheapest power flows would **overload a line**. **Redispatch**: the TSO pays one plant down and another (on the right side of the constraint) up to relieve it. Its cost has soared as renewables sit far from demand.

cards.front: The **N-1 security criterion** requires that the grid…
choices: Survives the loss of any single element without cascading
cards.back: N-1 means losing any one component (line, transformer, generator) must not cause a cascade — the core reliability standard that drives spare capacity.

choices: Zonal = one price per zone (congestion via redispatch); nodal = a price at every node reflecting local congestion
Zonal is only for gas; nodal only for solar
cards.back: Europe is mostly **zonal** (internal congestion handled out-of-market by redispatch); much of the US is **nodal/LMP**, pricing congestion at each node and signalling where to site.

cards.front: Why is the **grid**, not generation, often the binding constraint today?
cards.back: Generation keeps getting cheaper, but projects (and large new loads) wait years in **connection queues**, and **congestion/redispatch** costs are rising. You can't use power you can't deliver or connect.

Site and operate data-centre/AI load as a **grid-aware, flexible resource**: place it where grid and renewable headroom exist, **co-locate** with generation, and use its flexibility to help **balance** the system — turning a heavy load into firming demand.

cards.front: Why are AI/cloud **data centres** a 'grid variable', not just a consumer?
choices: They're large, often siteable, and partly flexible (can shift/curtail load)
cards.back: Because they're huge, frequently free to locate, and partly flexible, data centres can be placed and operated to *help* the grid (demand response, soaking up curtailed renewables) — or to strain it.
Generation or storage on the **customer's side** of the grid connection (e.g. a solar array or battery serving an on-site data centre). It reshapes or reduces the load the grid actually sees.
